summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide under the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which passed the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and was signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. The statute invalidates any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex and carries a maximum penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916.

Akwa Ibom stands under that secular national framework. The state lies outside the twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, so the death-penalty layer does not reach it and the ceiling for same-sex sexual activity in Akwa Ibom is 14 years' imprisonment. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) records no state-specific enforcement divergence: the national criminal framework applies across all states, and no evidence of a distinct Akwa Ibom enforcement pattern appears in the sources.

The 2014 Act reaches well beyond marriage. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, states that the Act also criminalises participants and guests at same-sex weddings, and warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) separately documents that the Act bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Gender identity carries no legal standing in Nigeria. The country has no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence against LGBT+ people is recorded countrywide. The UK Home Office note documents a pattern of arrests, detention and mob violence. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Police extortion on suspicion of homosexuality is also documented: in March 2025 Lagos police struck a 24-year-old man in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The FCDO advisory likewise warns of blackmail and intimidation alongside the risk of imprisonment.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The death-penalty layer that does not reach Akwa Ibom is active elsewhere in Nigeria. The twelve northern states operating Shari'a penal codes impose penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning. A Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and a further death-by-stoning sentence was reported from Bauchi in May 2024. In January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial.

The FCDO advisory reported in August 2026 frames the risk in the same terms the sources use for the north: up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity federally, with death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states. Travellers moving through Nigeria should treat the two layers as geographically distinct rather than as a single national risk.

Criminalisation has colonial-era roots. Nigeria's LGBTQ+ legal regime was reinforced by the 2014 statute on top of provisions dating to 1916, and the Act's reach into weddings, cohabitation and public expression means that conduct with no direct sexual element can still attract charges.
localsOnly:
Residents of Akwa Ibom live under the same 14-year ceiling as visitors, with no state-level protection layered over the national statute. Nigeria offers no anti-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so employment, housing and service disputes arising from trans status have no statutory remedy.

Gender identity is not legally recognised. A resident cannot obtain official documents reflecting a gender other than the one assigned at birth under any national provision recorded in these sources, and no framework exists for legal name or marker change.

Same-sex relationships receive no recognition, and the 2014 Act's bans on cohabitation between same-sex partners, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship and operation of gay organisations apply to residents in Akwa Ibom as elsewhere in the federation. Mob violence and police detention are recorded as countrywide harm patterns rather than as phenomena confined to any one state.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted remains unresolved. The sources available here neither confirm nor deny their current legal status.

No Akwa Ibom-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory. The claim that the state shows no enforcement divergence from the national framework rests on the UK Home Office note's silence on state-level variation, which is an absence of documented divergence rather than a positive finding of uniform practice.

Outcomes after the October 2024 panel's finding on Bobrisky's prison placement are not sourced, and the sources do not record whether the Bauchi stoning sentences were carried out or ratified.

The sources do not address access to gender-affirming healthcare, ID document rules at Akwa Ibom's airports or borders, or the practical availability of legal representation for trans detainees in the state.
